title: SYSK Selects: What Makes us Yawn?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of an episode on yawning, introduced by Josh as his pick. The hosts discuss why people yawn and why the cause is still unexplained: yawning is involuntary and seen in fetuses from about 11 to 20 weeks, so the oxygen theory fails; a rare brain lesion case shows yawns can still lift a paralyzed arm; yawns are linked to shifts in arousal and neurotransmitters; Robert Provine tested the oxygen and carbon dioxide ideas and found them wrong; theories include boredom, evolutionary signaling, and brain cooling (the leading view); contagious yawning is linked to empathy and mirror neurons, with studies on autism that the hosts question; Hippocrates' fever idea and seventeenth-century alertness views; outdoor temperature effects on yawning. The episode closes with a listener mail about Rodriguez, the singer-songwriter, and a recommendation of documentaries.
topics: oxygen and carbon dioxide yawning theory

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode on yawning. The hosts open with banter about chairs, Florida smear campaigns using technical terms, and pendiculating (stretching while yawning).

segments.title: Contagious yawning and involuntary yawns
segments.summary: Yawning is contagious, even among animals, and the hosts describe how reading or hearing about yawns triggers them. Yawning is involuntary, and fetuses have been observed yawning from about 11 to 20 weeks, which undercuts the oxygen theory. A rare brain lesion case shows yawns can still raise a paralyzed arm.

segments.title: Yawn mechanics and arousal
segments.summary: A yawn involves opening the mouth, inhaling, often closing the eyes, and stretching. Neurotransmitters and dopamine are activated. Robert Provine sees yawns as marking a shift between arousal states, and surfactant distribution in the lungs is mentioned. Yawning appears with nervousness and in animals, and Olympians have been seen yawning before races.

segments.title: Theories of why we yawn: oxygen, carbon dioxide, boredom
segments.summary: The hosts review theories. Provine tested the oxygen idea by giving athletes oxygen and raising carbon dioxide in ambient air, and yawning did not decrease. The boredom theory was dismissed by casual observation. Group yawning is discussed as a possible result of competition for oxygen, which the hosts doubt.

segments.title: Evolutionary theories and brain cooling
segments.summary: Evolutionary ideas include yawning as a display of teeth to intimidate and as a signal to group members. The brain cooling theory is described as the most recent and most widely favored, with warmer brains yawning to cool down for better thinking.

segments.title: Empathy, mirror neurons and autism studies
segments.summary: Contagious yawning is linked to empathy, and Provine's MRI studies suggest mirror neurons fire when people see yawns. Studies report that autistic people yawn less contagiously, though the hosts question the data, noting autistic people may focus on mouths rather than eyes.

segments.title: History of yawning theories and temperature effects
segments.summary: Hippocrates thought yawning was fever-related, an idea later disproven. Seventeenth and eighteenth century ideas tied yawning to alertness. Heart rate rises during yawns. Gallup and colleagues found outdoor temperature affects yawning frequency, and brain temperature also matters.

segments.title: Yawning as unsolved mystery and shared origins with orgasm
segments.summary: The hosts conclude yawning remains unexplained. Provine suggests yawns and orgasms share a neurobehavioral heritage. The hosts note they did not pick a single theory and joke about pets.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A brief sponsor message interrupts the episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: Rodriguez in Detroit
segments.summary: Julia recalls meeting Rodriguez at a Detroit bar in 2007, who played her a new song three times at a picnic table outside her apartment. She mentions the documentary Searching for Sugar Man and recommends No Place on Earth and How to Survive a Plague.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point to social media and the website.
